(1) the Arctic sea ice trends and the AO and ESO trends are related, (2) there are large regional differences between the AO and ESN0 effects on the ice trends, (3) the ice trends are larger than the ice changes associated the AO and ESS0, and (4) more local or less known large scale processes must be investigated to explain the trends.

the Arctic sea ice concentration trends are not consistent with the Arctic Oscillation trend, and that the Arctic Oscillation is not a good predictor of Arctic sea ice concentrations.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Arctic sea ice changes over the last two decades have been influenced by the AO, ENSO and other processes, which have caused the ice changes to be more pronounced in the western than eastern Arctic.
the Arctic Oscillation is a dominant factor in the Arctic sea ice variability, but the El Nino Southern oscillation is a secondary factor in the Arctic ice variability.

the AO and E N S O are the dominant large scale processes affecting the Arctic ice cover, and the AO and the ENSOs have been trending toward their positive and negative phases respectively over the past few decades.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Arctic sea ice variability is not only influenced by the large scale climate variability, but that the large scale variability can also be used to help interpret the observed regional ice changes.
the AO and E N SO have the potential to explain a significant portion of the recent Arctic sea ice variability, especially in the Bering, Barents/Kar a and Beaufort seas.
the ice trends in the western Arctic are related to a combination of the positive AO trend (which has been in place for 50 years) and a recent negative ENSO phase.
